title: Fill-Level Sensors for Remote Vault Toilets
one_liner: Satellite-capable fill-level and usage sensors for the vault toilets on public land and in campgrounds, so pump trucks go where and when they are actually needed.
customer: Campground and recreation concessionaires operating on federal and state land, state park systems, county park departments, ski areas and trailhead managers. Second wave: event, construction and portable-restroom fleets. Pumping contractors are channel partners.
problem: Vault toilets are pumped on fixed calendars or when a hiker reports an overflow. Busy sites need pumping weekly or monthly in peak season and remote sites once every year or two. Trucks drive one to three hours each way. A full toilet closes a site, damages the visitor experience, and holiday weekends generate emergency call-outs at premium rates.
solution: An ultrasonic or time-of-flight sensor puck under the riser lid plus a PIR visit counter, on LTE-M with a narrowband satellite (NB-NTN) fallback for no-coverage sites. The dashboard forecasts 'days to full' from usage and holiday and weather calendars, then auto-generates work orders to the nearest contractor with route batching. Usage counts also drive restocking of toilet paper and cleaning visits.
why_now: Narrowband satellite IoT modules and plans have reached commercial availability, cutting the cost of monitoring a toilet 40 miles from cell coverage. Recreation agencies and concessionaires face tight staffing and budgets, so triaging truck rolls has real value.
revenue_model: USD 12-20 per toilet per month including a leased sensor (about USD 150 hardware cost). A 600-toilet concessionaire is about USD 100k per year. Route-optimization module for pumpers. Event-fleet pricing per unit per event.
non_obvious_insight: The savings isn't fewer pump-outs; it's knowing which toilets are near-full before a holiday weekend and avoiding closures and emergency call-outs. Pumpers earn per visit, so pitch them a route-density and demand-forecast tool that grows their business rather than threatening it.
first_30_days: Build 30 units from off-the-shelf modules. Pilot 5-10 toilets each with three concessionaires and two county park departments. Use the shoulder season (hunting and early winter trailheads) to test. Recruit one septic pumping company as a co-pilot partner. Convert to annual contracts before next spring's opening.

title: Licensed Cozy Games for Memory Care
one_liner: A turnkey activity program for senior living made of commercially licensed cozy indie games, in a kiosk kit that logs resident participation for compliance paperwork.
customer: Activity directors and operators of memory care, assisted living and skilled nursing communities, starting with independents and small regional chains of 5-50 sites. They pay about $199-349 a month per community plus a $349-499 kit.
problem: Nursing homes must run person-centered activity programs and document participation (CMS F-tag 679). Directors are short on budget and staff time. Existing tech is expensive proprietary hardware such as projector tables or VR. Consumer games are the wrong fit: their licences forbid commercial and public use, and they have reading-heavy UI, timers and fail states.
solution: A curated library of 30-50 indie titles that are gentle by design: no fail states, no timers, big targets, little text, familiar themes like gardening, cooking and tidying. Developers grant commercial, DRM-free licences for a revenue share. Each title runs in a locked kiosk launcher on a docked handheld or mini-PC to the TV, with big-button controllers. Staff get 5-minute group-play cards and a one-tap participation log that exports to activity documentation. It is positioned as activity programming, not therapy, so it makes no clinical claims.
why_now: About 4M Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, so demand for senior activities is rising. Handheld PCs are cheap and reliable. Senior living operators are already piloting games (for example the Belmont Village pilot of a cognitive game). Steam's glut of cozy games means many strong titles with dormant back-catalogs that earn nothing.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription per community, a hardware kit margin, and 40-50% of subscription revenue paid to developers by playtime. Later: enterprise contracts with chains, and reimbursement or wellness-budget channels.
non_obvious_insight: Steam keys are personal-use licences. Only the developer can grant commercial or public-performance rights, and a dormant catalog makes them say yes for a small guarantee. The traits that make cozy games sell are exactly what dementia-friendly design needs. And directors buy relief from documentation and set-up time, not cognitive outcomes. VCs file this under 'brain-training edtech', while an insider sees a licensing arbitrage plus a compliance workflow.
first_30_days: License 8-10 cozy titles, offering $500 minimum guarantees plus revenue share. Assemble 5 kits at about $400 each. Offer free 4-week pilots to 5 local communities through activity-director Facebook groups and state activity-professional associations. Log participation minutes per resident. Convert pilots to paid at week 5.

title: Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases
one_liner: White-label filing infrastructure that lets solo immigration lawyers file mandamus/APA delay lawsuits in 48 hours, turning the government's habit of mooting suits into a flat-fee product.
customer: Solo and small immigration firms (1-10 attorneys) who pay a per-filing platform fee; end clients (naturalization, green card and employment petition applicants) pay the firm a flat $2.5-5k. Secondary buyer: employers with stuck petitions.
problem: Cases are stuck well past posted processing times: interviewed N-400s never scheduled for oath, I-485s and I-140s idling, and holds or pauses applied to nationals of dozens of countries since late 2025. Clients wait 12-30 months. Lawyers know a federal delay suit often shakes a case loose, but most solos have never filed one. Drafting the complaint, civil cover sheet, summons, service on the U.S. Attorney's civil process clerk, the Attorney General and the agency, and district-specific local rules is a 6-10 hour learning curve, and no one wants to be the first to file.
solution: A web tool with three parts. (1) An eligibility screen: enter the receipt date, form type and field office, and it compares them to posted times and to real observed outcomes, then scores the delay claim. (2) A complaint and exhibit generator with a per-district rules library, a service-of-process checklist and deadline calendar (the 60-day government answer window), and a template for the joint status report or stipulated dismissal that follows adjudication. (3) A docket-outcome database that logs, by district, judge and case type, how long from filing to adjudication. The attorney of record signs every filing. The platform is software, not a law firm.
why_now: Through late 2025 and 2026 USCIS added enhanced vetting, holds and pauses on benefit requests tied to nationality, expanded re-review of approved cases, and slower naturalization and green card scheduling. The volume of genuinely stuck cases is at a decade high. Federal courts are also less deferential to agencies since the Loper Bright decision, and adjudicating a stuck case is cheaper for the government than defending it. Solos are overloaded and short of billable-hour alternatives, so a ready-made product for a high-ticket service is easy to sell.
revenue_model: $350-600 per filing charged to the law firm (flat, not a percentage, to avoid fee-splitting rules), or $299/month for up to 3 filings. Later: a paid intelligence tier of docket-outcome analytics by district, and a litigation-funding partnership for clients who can't front the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit is rarely litigated to judgment. The U.S. Attorney's Office usually tells USCIS to adjudicate within 30-90 days so the suit can be dismissed as moot, so the client's real purchase is a forced deadline. Clients almost never hear about this because form-prep firms earn on the application, not on pressure. Posted processing times are also misleading (they reflect only completed cases at a percentile), so whoever accumulates real time-to-decision data by field office and district owns the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 immigration attorneys in high-volume districts (N.D. Cal., S.D. Tex., D.N.J., E.D.N.Y., S.D. Fla.) and offer free templates for the first filing. Build the intake screen and three complaint templates first (delayed N-400 after interview, delayed I-485, delayed I-130/I-140 or a nationality hold). Concierge-run 10 filings by hand, charging the firms $400 each. Log every outcome date, since that dataset is the product. Post outcome stats to immigration-lawyer Facebook groups and AILA chapter listservs to pull in the next 30 firms.

title: Triage Software for Satellite-SOS Rescue Teams
one_liner: Intake, deduplication and dispatch software for county and volunteer search-and-rescue teams flooded by satellite SOS messages.
customer: County sheriff SAR coordinators, state SAR coordinators, national park services and mountain rescue organizations.
problem: As satellite texting reaches ordinary phones, more people go remote and press SOS. Rescuers receive short, delayed, asynchronous messages with weak location data and many false alarms. Coordination centers were built for 911 voice calls, and volunteer teams run on spreadsheets and group texts.
solution: A gateway that ingests SOS relays (email, API, text) from phone makers and satellite messaging providers, deduplicates, geolocates, and adds terrain and weather context. It runs structured 160-character question flows, recommends the resource type to dispatch, and keeps a log for after-action review and cost recovery.
why_now: Satellite messaging on unmodified phones went mainstream across 2025-26 (the briefing shows new carrier launches as late as Sept 28, 2026). AST and SpaceX D2C are scaling, and phone makers are adding satellite SOS. The receiving end has not been rebuilt.
revenue_model: $3-15k per year per county or team. State-level contracts of $50-200k. Optional paid membership or SAR-insurance partnership.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck moved from sending distress to receiving and triaging it. Whoever owns the receive-side workflow becomes the system of record, and public agencies pay for it out of existing rescue budgets.
first_30_days: Shadow three volunteer SAR teams and one state coordinator. Build a minimal intake and dedupe tool that runs alongside their current tools. Offer it free for one summer season in exchange for a paid annual contract.

title: Airline-Grade Depot Maintenance for Drone Fleets
one_liner: A swap-based depot and records service that applies airline maintenance discipline to police drone-as-first-responder, ag-spray and utility inspection fleets.
customer: Sheriff's offices and municipal police and fire departments running 5-30 docked drones, agricultural spray operators, and utility and rail inspection contractors. The buyer is the program manager or operations lead, paying per airframe per month.
problem: Drone programs are run by one enthusiastic officer or a few pilots. Flying is the easy part. The real risks are battery cycle counts and swelling, motor and prop wear, firmware drift across a fleet, undocumented crash repairs, and no clear rule for when an aircraft is airworthy enough to dispatch. Aircraft techs recognize all of it: life-limited parts, configuration control, intermittent faults, 'no fault found', and sign-off traceability. Agencies also need records that survive scrutiny in court or after an incident. Manufacturer service plans cover their own hardware only and are mostly warranty repair, not fleet discipline.
solution: A monthly airframe subscription that includes a rotable-style exchange pool. When something fails, we ship an airworthy replacement airframe, gimbal or battery set overnight and take the broken one to our bench, so the program is never down. We keep per-airframe and per-battery records with QR codes, cycle counts and firmware baselines. We run a pre-deployment inspection checklist that acts like a simple minimum-equipment list for dispatch. Records are exported in evidentiary format. Techs staffing the bench are retired or moonlighting A&Ps.
why_now: The 2025 White House drone executive order and the FAA's proposed BVLOS rule (Part 108) point toward large fleets flying beyond visual line of sight, and hundreds of US police and fire departments are standing up drone-as-first-responder programs. Tightening US restrictions on Chinese-made drone equipment mean installed fleets must be kept flying for years while spare parts get scarce, which makes maintenance skill a moat. Mechanic supply is also loosening at the edges as retired A&Ps look for part-time work.
revenue_model: $450-900 per airframe per month for the exchange and records subscription, fixed-fee inspections ($150 per airframe), battery-audit fees, parts margin on refurbished airframes, and later a training and certification product for agency pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Drone programs will relearn every airline lesson, and the money is in configuration control and records, not in flying. A rotable exchange pool beats field repair because the customer's real pain is downtime and liability, not the repair cost. Manufacturers mostly sell to fleets of one brand, but real fleets are multi-vendor, so an independent depot with an airline-style record system has room to win.
first_30_days: Pick one metro and sign three agencies or ag operators to a discounted pilot at $450 per airframe per month. Set up a bench in a rented hangar bay or garage with two part-time A&Ps. Run the record system on Airtable with QR labels, and sell battery-health audits and pre-deployment inspections at fixed prices as the first paid products. Use an airline-style monthly 'fleet status' report as the marketing piece. By day 30, the target is at least one signed agreement and a small exchange pool of two spare airframes.

title: Independent Accuracy Certification for Wearable Health Claims
one_liner: A third-party lab that certifies wearable metrics (HRV, sleep staging, BP trends) now that the FDA has stepped back, funded by makers and trusted by buyers.
customer: Wearable and health-app makers selling into employers, payers, clinics, coaches and gyms (they pay for certification). Secondary: self-insured employers, payers and coaching platforms that subscribe to procurement-grade reports.
problem: Insiders cheered the FDA's January 2026 General Wellness guidance as freedom. But no clearance means no trusted filter: buyers cannot tell which of dozens of rings, watches and patches are accurate, one analysis argued wearables 'beat the FDA and lost the insurance money', and makers have no credible third-party proof to show payers. Claims exposure to the FTC, state AGs and class actions rises at the same time.
solution: Run a standing panel of about 200 volunteers with lab-grade references (ECG chest strap, a partner polysomnography lab, clinical and ambulatory BP, VO2/lactate testing). Test devices and features under a published protocol, issue tiered 'Verified for [metric]' marks with stated error bands (re-tested at major firmware changes), publish a public leaderboard, and sell buyers a procurement report they can cite in RFPs.
why_now: FDA's Jan 2026 wellness guidance lets physiologic-metric features (HRV, SpO2, BP trends) skip review; Whoop's BP feature drew a July 2025 warning letter and a June 2026 closeout; the HIPRA consumer-health-data bill cleared Senate HELP 22-0 on July 30, 2026, so scrutiny of wearable data is rising while the FDA filter is gone.
revenue_model: Certification fees of $15-60k per device or feature per year with re-test fees; $5-25k/yr buyer subscriptions for procurement reports; per-test fees for startups needing payer credibility.
non_obvious_insight: Deregulation does not remove the need for a trust filter, it privatizes it. The certifier is paid by makers but its only currency is buyer trust, so it must publish unflattering results (Consumer Reports crossed with a safety-lab model). Whoever writes the reference protocol first gets cited in payer and employer RFPs, which is a durable moat.
first_30_days: Partner with a university exercise-physiology or sleep lab, recruit 40 volunteers, test 6 popular rings/watches on resting HR, HRV and sleep staging against ECG/PSG, publish the methodology and preliminary results, then sell 2-3 employer-facing wearable startups a paid $15k pre-publication verification.

title: Dementia Desk: Ex-Aide Call Center for Banks
one_liner: A remote call-center pod staffed by former dementia aides, taking the confused, repeat and possibly scammed callers that credit unions and utilities cannot handle.
customer: Credit unions ($200M-$3B assets), regional banks, municipal and regional utilities, and pharmacy chains' member-service teams. The compliance or member-experience officer signs. Medicare Advantage plan call centers are the second wave.
problem: Front-line agents are scored on handle time. A caller with dementia asks the same question nine times, fails the security questions, insists a dead husband is in the room, or is being coached by a scammer sitting beside them. Agents correct them, hang up or escalate. That distresses the caller, costs the institution money and produces fraud losses. Free training exists (AARP BankSafe videos), but nobody takes the hard calls.
solution: A warm-transfer line. The agent presses a button on any call that sounds impaired and a Dementia Desk specialist takes over within seconds. Specialists are ex-aides with 5-15 years in dementia care. They use the aide toolkit: join the caller's reality, don't correct, redirect, never argue about facts, and verify later with the trusted contact. They can also tell when a second voice is coaching. Each call ends with a structured note: risk flag, trusted-contact action, card freeze, callback plan. The service also hands the institution documented staff training for the Senior Safe Act.
why_now: The oldest boomers turn 80 in 2026, so vulnerable callers are rising fast. AI voice-clone scams against elders spiked in 2025-26. The Senior Safe Act (12 USC 3423) grants a bank immunity for reporting suspected exploitation only if the staff were trained and the training is documented. Home care aides are leaving the field with back injuries and low pay, and remote work at $20-24 per hour is a real second career for them.
revenue_model: $9-14 per handled contact with a $2,000 monthly minimum. A $4 per employee per year Senior Safe Act training add-on. Later, a per-account fee for a 'trusted contact enrollment' outbound program that reduces fraud losses.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not detection. Institutions already know who's confused. The problem is that nobody on the phone knows what to do next and every training video is passive. The scarce skill is de-escalating cognitively impaired adults, and the only people who have it at scale are underpaid home aides. This turns the labor supply that home care has been losing into a premium BPO product, and it gives aides a career path off their spines.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 ex-aides from CNA and HHA school alumni groups and caregiver Facebook groups. Write a 12-page call playbook from their own scripts. Offer two local credit unions a free 60-day pilot: agents warm-transfer any call they flag to a Google Voice line the pod answers, with a monthly report of fraud saves. Charge from month three. Ask the state credit union league to host a 30-minute 'confused caller' webinar as the lead source.

title: All-In Site Quotes for Chassis-Free Homes
one_liner: Type a parcel address, get a fixed-price foundation, utility-hookup and permit package for a factory-built home, delivered by a local crew network.
customer: Manufactured and modular home dealers, small landowners and buyers, and factory builders that need site-work partners. Rural and small-town jurisdictions benefit indirectly.
problem: The ROAD to Housing Act (signed July 11, 2026) kills the steel-chassis rule, worth about $10K or 10% of unit cost, though HUD must still publish standards. Cheaper units will ship, but the sale is decided by unknown site costs: foundation, utilities, septic or well, set crew and permits. These stay local and human, and dealers cannot quote the all-in price.
solution: A parcel-level site-cost estimator using soils, flood zone, utility distance, jurisdiction fees and foundation type, returning a fixed-price quote in 24 hours. It is backed by a vetted crew network (excavation, foundation, set, utilities) on 7-day pay, one accountable contract, and packaged construction-to-perm financing. Begin with conventional manufactured homes on permanent foundations, so revenue starts before HUD standards land.
why_now: ROAD Act enacted July 2026 with HUD standards pending and a federal showcase of factory-built homes. Site work is exactly where the labor shortage and permit friction bite hardest. Standard duplex and townhome blueprints are being funded.
revenue_model: 10-15% GC margin on site packages ($30-60K). $300-500 quote fee credited on booking. Dealer referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone watching the ROAD Act watches factories and financing. The bottleneck will be the last 100 feet, and price uncertainty there kills the cheap-home pitch. The first team that gives a real all-in number becomes the dealers' default site partner and captures the margin the factory cannot.
first_30_days: Choose a county cluster in Texas or the Southeast where manufactured homes are common. Sign two dealers. Build the estimator from public GIS, flood and utility data. Deliver 20 free quotes and convert 2-3 to jobs with existing subs.

title: Revocation List for Leaked ID Documents
one_liner: A neutral, hashed registry of compromised license and passport records that every verifier can check, forcing step-up on IDs from the Nexus/IDScan.net dump.
customer: IDV and KYC vendors, marketplaces, gig platforms, neobanks, telecom and car-rental retail, and lenders, buying an API.
problem: On Aug 31 2026 the Nexus market began selling 153M+ US and Canadian driver's licenses, each with six images including infrared and ultraviolet scans. Researchers call stored ID images 'permanent fraud tools'. Verifiers cannot tell a fresh scan from a leaked record, and issuers will not revoke tens of millions of licenses.
solution: Ingest breach corpora only through controlled, lawful channels (researcher and law-enforcement partners, hash-only contributions). Compute privacy-preserving fingerprints (salted hashes of document number, state and DOB combinations, and perceptual hashes of portraits). Expose an API answering 'has this document instance been seen compromised?' with a risk tier and recommended step-up (mobile ID, bank-account link, in-person). Add hash-prefix consumer lookup and DMV reissue guidance.
why_now: The Nexus dump is the biggest leak of ID scans and follows 2025 leaks of ID photos from age-verification and support systems (e.g., Discord's vendor). Document-image KYC now needs a compensating signal, and verifiers have none.
revenue_model: $0.01-0.05 per check or $2-20K per month subscriptions, with consumer-alert partnerships through banks.
non_obvious_insight: Public-key infrastructure solved 'a trusted key was stolen' with revocation lists, not by preventing theft. Issuers will not revoke documents, but verifiers can pool what they know. The leak itself is the data source, and the value comes from the shared list.
first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 breach researchers and one small IDV vendor. Build the hashing pipeline and API, and clear the design with privacy counsel. Give it free to 10 verifiers, then convert by usage.

title: AI Standardized Clients for Counseling Programs
one_liner: Voice-based AI 'clients' with persistent backstories, scored on accredited-skills rubrics, give master's students hundreds of rehearsal sessions before real practicum.
customer: Counseling, social-work and MFT master's programs (CACREP-accredited and similar), then OT and PT programs for patient-interview training; the department or a student lab fee pays.
problem: Practicum placements and faculty supervision are scarce. Human standardized clients cost about $30-60 an hour, and classmate role-plays are low fidelity. The new loan caps squeeze programs in excluded fields, and students need repetitions in high-stakes skills like suicide-risk assessment and motivational interviewing.
solution: Real-time voice client agents that stay consistent across sessions, remember last week, vary in difficulty and present safety-critical scenarios. Sessions are auto-scored on rubrics (reflective listening, risk questions asked, missed cues), supervisors review flagged clips, and sessions are logged as pre-practicum skills hours. Rehearsal volume is multiplied, not supervised hours replaced.
why_now: Low-latency, natural voice models with long-term memory reached usable fidelity in 2025-26. Programs in excluded fields face cost pressure after July 2026, and therapist demand remains strong.
revenue_model: $75-200 per student per semester as a lab fee, or $15-40k site licenses per program.
non_obvious_insight: What was infeasible was a client who stays consistent over sessions and reacts with emotion in real time. The binding constraint in clinical training is rehearsal volume, which is exactly what AI supplies cheaply, without threatening the human-supervised hours that licensure requires.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 counseling programs through adjunct faculty who teach skills labs. Build 6 scenarios (intake, motivational interviewing, suicide risk) and run a spring pilot. Measure improvement on the program's existing skills rubric and price at about $100 per student. Build in clinical safety review and privacy controls.

title: Exchange for Shelved Academic Projects and Null Data
one_liner: Buy the 'graveyard' of academic labs, meaning abandoned projects, validated knockout lines, half-built assays and failed-experiment data, and resell them as dossiers with an interview slot to seed biotechs and AI-bio data teams. Supply is anchored by a paid lab-closure clearance service.
customer: Sellers: departing postdocs, PIs downsizing or closing labs, and department chairs and EHS offices who must clear the space. Buyers: seed biotech founders, AI-bio and virtual-cell model companies that need experimental data including null results, pharma target-validation groups, and CROs that need validated cell models. Dossiers sell for $3-30k, and closure concierge fees run $5-15k.
problem: Every lab has a graveyard: KO lines, reporter constructs, a half-optimized assay, a screen that didn't pan out, and boxes in the -80 labeled 'JK 3/14 P3 #2'. When a postdoc leaves or a lab shrinks, the physical items are discarded or become orphaned, and the reasons the project failed leave in the postdoc's head. Meanwhile a startup or AI-bio team pays 12 months and $500k to rebuild the same tools and rediscover the same dead ends. Published literature is heavily biased toward positives, and models trained only on positives are systematically overconfident.
solution: Two-sided wedge. Supply side: 'Lab Closure Concierge' is a fixed-fee triage service for labs that are closing or downsizing. It inventories freezers, plasmids, cell lines and mouse lines, interviews the departing postdoc for 90 minutes to capture provenance and failure reasons (transcribed and structured with AI), disposes of hazardous items compliantly, and flags what is worth keeping. Demand side: a curated catalog of 'dossiers': the physical or digital assets, protocols, raw data including nulls, plus a paid call with the person who built them. Use a standard institutional license or MTA template with a revenue share to the university, so overloaded tech-transfer offices approve it because the alternative is a dumpster.
why_now: NIH grant terminations, indirect-cost fights and uncertain 2026 budgets are pushing labs to shrink or close. Biotech shutdowns have also left surplus bench assets (verify current scale). AI-bio companies are openly short of high-quality experimental data, especially negative data, and pay for it. Tech-transfer offices are understaffed. LLM transcription and structuring turns a 90-minute interview into a searchable dossier cheaply.
revenue_model: Closure-concierge flat fee paid by the department or PI. A 25-30% commission on dossier sales, with revenue share to seller and institution. Annual data-subscription tier for AI-bio buyers (curated null-result feeds).
non_obvious_insight: The vials are worth very little. The value is provenance plus the 'why it failed' story stored in one person's memory, and it evaporates the day the postdoc's visa or contract ends. So the product is not a marketplace for samples, it is structured exit-knowledge capture with a physical-asset appendix. Because the university owns the IP anyway, the clean structure is to make the institution a paid party rather than an obstacle.
first_30_days: Use your own postdoc network to line up 3-5 labs that are shrinking or have departing postdocs. Offer a free triage-and-catalog audit in exchange for permission to list a few assets. Produce 10 dossiers with structured interviews. Cold-email 30 seed biotechs and AI-bio data leads with the top 5 dossiers. Close one sale at $3-8k. Use that transaction to test the university revenue-share template with one tech-transfer office.

title: ARIA Watch: Aide Eyes for Alzheimer's Drug Clinics
one_liner: A 60-second daily safety check done by the home aide or family for patients on anti-amyloid drugs, flagging the subtle change that precedes brain-swelling side effects, sold to the memory clinic that prescribes them.
customer: Neurology and memory practices and infusion or injection programs running Leqembi and Kisunla. The buyer is the practice manager or program nurse coordinator. The revenue partner is the patient's home care agency.
problem: Anti-amyloid drugs carry ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding) risk, mostly caught by MRI at scheduled points. Symptoms such as headache, dizziness, vision change, new confusion or seizures often appear between scans. A person with dementia cannot report them. The infusion nurse sees the patient for two hours every two weeks and cannot judge baseline. The person who can is the aide, who sees the patient every morning and says 'she's not herself today.' Nobody asks the aide.
solution: A structured, plain-language daily check on a phone, with a voice option in the aide's language. It records a few observations against the patient's own baseline: gait, speech, new headache behavior, appetite, alertness and a free-text 'not herself'. A protocol turns 'change from baseline' into three levels: log, call the nurse today, or send to the ED. Alerts land in the clinic's inbox with a timeline. Aides get a small per-check stipend. The agency gets a revenue share. The practice gets documentation for safety programs and the patient-family peace of mind that keeps them on therapy.
why_now: The FDA approved Leqembi Iqlik, a home-administered subcutaneous starting dose, in July 2026, with launch in late August. Fewer infusion visits means fewer clinician touchpoints, while MRI-based ARIA monitoring remains. FDA-cleared blood tests are increasing the number of treated patients. CMS finalized new 2026 remote-monitoring codes for 2-15 days of data (99445) and the first 10 minutes of management (99470), making light-touch programs billable. Self-reported observations alone do not qualify for RPM, so the model pairs with a connected BP or pulse-ox device or bills through care-management routes such as CCM, PCM or GUIDE.
revenue_model: $45-65 per patient per month paid by the practice. A $10-15 per month stipend to the aide or agency comes out of that. Optional device add-on to unlock RPM billing. Later, pharma-funded real-world safety and function studies drawn from the aide-observed baseline data.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable clinical sensor for a patient who cannot self-report is the person who changes their sheets. Aide phrasing like 'not herself' or 'slower' is a better early signal than a symptom checklist the patient can't complete, and it arrives as a behavior change, not a complaint. Home care agencies have always been treated as a cost center by clinics. Here they become a data channel that clinics will pay for.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 memory clinic nurse coordinators and two infusion-center managers and ask what they do between MRIs. Build the check as a no-login web form and SMS. Recruit 3 agencies whose clients are on Leqembi or Kisunla, plus a neurologist champion. Offer a free 90-day pilot on 15 patients, with a monthly report of flags raised and calls avoided. Convert to per-patient pricing once one true early catch is documented.

title: Remote Operator-of-Record for Small Water Systems
one_liner: A roll-up of certified operator licenses and contracts, with cheap remote telemetry so one operator can be operator-of-record for 10-30 small systems.
customer: Small towns, rural water districts, mobile-home and RV parks, HOAs and private systems in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Oklahoma and Iowa. The system pays a monthly fee, and state technical-assistance funds can help.
problem: State law requires a certified operator in responsible charge, yet operators are retiring and small systems cannot hire. Missed sampling and reporting cause violations. The 2027 PFAS initial monitoring and the LCRI lead changes (action level tightens Nov 1, 2027) add workload that these systems cannot absorb.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired operators as a paid bench. Install cellular SCADA gateways ($1-3k hardware) and a compliance calendar (sampling, consumer confidence reports, PFAS and lead tasks). Add on-call field technicians. Start with states that allow remote responsible charge, and with private systems where the sales cycle is shortest.
why_now: The retirement wave, the 2027 monitoring and lead deadlines, $7.2B in FY2026 revolving-fund money (some for small-system assistance), and cheap remote telemetry all coincide.
revenue_model: $3-12k/month per system, plus a compliance-concierge upsell for PFAS and lead sampling packages.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation requires a licensed human, not a plant, so the scarce asset is license-hours. Remote monitoring multiplies each license roughly tenfold. The roll-up is of licenses and contracts, not of plants.
first_30_days: Recruit three retired Grade 2-4 operators. Sign five private systems (mobile-home park owners first). Partner with a state rural water association for referrals. Confirm your state's rules on remote responsible charge with the regulator before selling.

title: Kennel Canary: Outbreak Surveillance for Dog Daycares
angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
one_liner: Monthly environmental PCR swabs that give dog daycares, boarders and shelters an early-warning system and proof of due diligence.
customer: Dog daycare, boarding, grooming and training facilities (independents and franchise systems), animal shelters, and the specialty insurers that cover pet-care businesses.
problem: Canine influenza, kennel-cough pathogens and parvo outbreaks force closures, trigger owner lawsuits and tarnish reputation, and a facility can lose 20-30% of a month's revenue in one event. Facilities rely on vaccination records and owner honesty, and testing individual dogs means a vet visit ($150-300) after symptoms appear, which is hard when vets are scarce and 85% of clients decline care above $1,000.
solution: Subscription sentinel kits: pooled air-filter and surface swabs shipped to a partner lab that runs automated multiplex qPCR (CIV, CPIV, CRCoV, Bordetella, Mycoplasma cynos, Strep zooepidemicus, parvo, distemper) with 24-48 hour turnaround. Facilities get a traffic-light dashboard, outbreak playbooks (isolate, sanitize, boost vaccination), and a 'verified-clean' badge for marketing. Insurers receive premium-credit pilots. Aggregated data becomes a regional canine disease early-warning map.
why_now: Post-COVID pet ownership and return-to-office have grown daycare and boarding. Human wastewater and airborne surveillance have matured, and automated extraction plus multiplex PCR have driven per-sample costs down. Regional canine flu and respiratory outbreaks recur, and clinics have less capacity to triage.
revenue_model: $149 per month for a small facility (bi-weekly swabs), $399 per month for multi-room sites, and $50-150k per year for franchise systems. Sample cost is $20-30 at scale. Insurer-paid pilots per insured location and a $10-30k per year data subscription for vaccine makers and veterinary groups.
non_obvious_insight: What these buyers purchase is liability and reputation protection, not health testing. A sentinel result is a dated due-diligence log that insurers and lawyers value, and one avoided closure pays for a year. Pathogen surveillance built for airports and cities has never been priced for the roughly 100,000-plus US pet-care sites.
first_30_days: Partner with a university or commercial vet diagnostic lab that already has a validated respiratory multiplex PCR. Sign 5 daycares via one franchise owner or local trade group for an 8-week pilot at $99 per month. Interview two specialty insurers about credits. Publish a short 'what we found in the air' report to generate inbound interest.

title: Old Job Kits for Dementia Sundown Hours
one_liner: A monthly subscription of dignified, occupation-matched 'work' boxes, such as a retired bookkeeper's ledger and receipts or a retired mechanic's hardware bench, that calm sundowning better than puzzles or toys. Aides earn referral commissions.
customer: Adult children caring for a parent with moderate dementia at home (about $34-44 per month), plus adult day programs and memory care activity directors who buy in bulk. The family pays.
problem: From 4 to 7pm many dementia patients get restless, pace and get aggressive. Families use the TV, memory games or, worse, sedatives. Toys and puzzles marketed to dementia patients often insult them; they toss the plush or refuse the coloring book. What actually calms most patients is purposeful work related to the life they used to have: the retired accountant sorting receipts, the teacher grading papers, the seamstress matching buttons, the waiter folding napkins, the farmer sorting seeds.
solution: Family fills out a 3-minute 'what did they do for work?' intake. Each month a box ships with real, adult-looking, safe materials for that career. Examples are a bookkeeper's ledger, adding-machine paper, a rubber stamp and pre-sorted stacks. A teacher gets a stack of old spelling tests with a red pen and gold stars. A mechanic gets large washers and nuts on a workbench tray. Nothing sharp, small or childlike. A card gives the aide or family a 30-second 'handoff line' ('the boss needs these sorted before five'). Aides get a personal referral code and 20 percent commission.
why_now: CMS's push to reduce antipsychotic use in dementia and its GUIDE dementia care model (live since July 2024, with caregiver education and respite requirements) push practices toward cheap non-drug behavior tools. Short-form video is a free channel, since a grandfather 'clocking in' to sort receipts is deeply shareable. Families are stretched by cuts to home care hours and turn to anything that buys them a calm evening.
revenue_model: $34-44 per month subscription with quarterly rotation. Bulk B2B orders of $250 per month per adult day or memory care program. 20 percent referral commissions to aides and care managers. Upsell to 'career library' add-ons and licensed professional-uniform accessories.
non_obvious_insight: The trick is not stimulation but purpose, and it must look like a real job, because anything that looks like a child's toy is rejected as an insult. Also, families ask their aide what to buy, and aides are the most trusted product recommenders in the house, yet no brand has ever paid them. Paying aides a commission creates a distribution channel no ad budget can match and quietly raises their income.
first_30_days: Build 6 career kits (bookkeeper, teacher, mechanic, seamstress, waiter, nurse) for under $18 each from restaurant-supply, office and hardware stores. Film 15 TikTok and Instagram clips with permission from families. Post in three large caregiver Facebook groups and offer 30 free kits in exchange for video testimonials. Give 20 aides referral codes. Sign up 3 local adult day centers for a $250 monthly pilot. Aim for 50 paying subscribers by day 60.

title: Canary Humans: Leak-Testing ID Verification Vendors
one_liner: Put consenting, instrumented real people through a platform's ID and age checks, then prove whether the vendor kept, leaked or resold their documents.
customer: Trust-and-safety, privacy and vendor-risk leads at platforms that outsource ID or age checks (dating apps, gig and rental marketplaces, cannabis and vape retail tech, crypto exchanges, adult and gaming operators), and the cyber insurers underwriting them.
problem: Platforms pick verification vendors on a SOC 2 badge and a promise to delete images quickly, and customers cannot test that promise. AU10TIX, Discord's support vendor, Persona and IDScan were all breached in 2024-26. IDScan reported 150M+ licence scans stolen in Sept 2026. Ofcom and state AGs judge platforms on 'reasonable steps', so the platform owns its vendor's failure.
solution: Recruit a few hundred paid 'canary humans' with unique emails, phones, addresses and ID numbers, and enrol them in the customer's live verification flow with the customer's consent. Then run scheduled tests: deletion requests, access requests to the vendor and its sub-processors, and monitoring of breach dumps, data-broker files, phishing and spam lists and dark-market listings for canary-unique strings. The deliverable is a quarterly retention and leakage attestation with evidence, usable in vendor contracts, cyber-insurance applications and regulator files. It also produces a public 'retention half-life' benchmark by vendor.
why_now: IDScan's Sept 2026 breach (150M+ licences) and the Persona, AU10TIX and Discord-vendor incidents showed that certified vendors leak. The EU's 31 Dec 2026 age-verification rollout deadline will push thousands more sites to outsource checks. Ofcom has opened 90+ investigations and issued fines. The Delve scandal (Mar-Apr 2026) showed that paper compliance is not proof.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per platform per vendor tested, an insurer portfolio programme (per-insured fee), and a breach-forensics retainer. Later add an efficacy-proof product for privacy-removal services.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance automation (Vanta is at roughly $300M ARR) certifies that controls exist on paper, and nobody tests outcomes. A verifier's product is a promise to forget, and the only way to audit a promise about data is to plant traceable data and watch where it surfaces. Security calls these honeytokens and direct marketers call them seed lists, but nobody has applied the trick to verification vendors.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 privacy-minded volunteers at $100-200 each with signed consent and a legal review (no fake IDs, real people only). Pitch three mid-size dating, gig or cannabis-tech platforms and one cyber MGA. Offer a free 90-day pilot against one vendor under NDA. Publish an anonymised benchmark from the pilot to generate inbound.

title: Offline Brain for Talking Toys
one_liner: A sub-$20 on-device speech-and-language module that lets toys hold child-safe conversations with no cloud, no audio leaving the toy and parent-readable summaries on the parent's phone.
customer: Toy brands and ODMs, indie AI-toy startups and kids' IP licensors who fear cloud data liability.
problem: Cloud-based AI toys stream children's voices to servers, which the amended COPPA rule (biometrics, retention limits, separate opt-in for third-party sharing) makes risky. Brand exposure is rising after consumer tests and lawsuits. Toy makers lack model-safety teams, and per-conversation cloud costs collide with a one-time hardware sale.
solution: A reference design and software stack: kid-tuned speech recognition, a 1-4B-parameter model fine-tuned for age-banded personas and refusals, and text-to-speech on a $10-15 NPU chip. Safety-locked story and play modes, and Bluetooth summaries to a parent app. Licensed to ODMs, with dev kits for startups.
why_now: Small on-device models reached conversational quality in 2025-26 and cheap NPUs run them in real time, so the technology only just became feasible. Regulation turns cloud audio into a liability, and holiday 2026 is the first big AI-toy season.
revenue_model: $2-4 per unit licence, $299 dev kits, and paid NRE for custom personas.
non_obvious_insight: The cloud is both the risk and the cost. On-device removes marginal cost and turns COPPA from a burden into a marketing claim ('nothing leaves the toy'), fixing the broken subscription-for-hardware model.
first_30_days: Prototype on a Raspberry Pi 5 or RK3588 board with an off-the-shelf small model. Measure latency and accuracy on consented child speech. Demo to 15 indie toy makers on Kickstarter and Crowd Supply and to 2 ODMs. Aim for 2 paid dev-kit pilots with $5k NRE each.

title: Pooled Radiation Test Data for Commercial Chips
one_liner: A subscription database and beam-time broker so satellite builders stop each paying to test the same commercial chips.
customer: Constellation and smallsat builders using commercial parts, defense new-space suppliers, and chip vendors seeking space design wins.
problem: Proliferated constellations (Golden Dome's reported 600-satellite award, Starlink) run on commercial parts. Radiation-beam slots are scarce with multi-month queues, and results live in silos. Roughly the same popular parts get tested repeatedly.
solution: Pool member orders to buy block beam time at university and national facilities, and test the top parts by lot and date code. Publish a member-contributed database of results and anomalies, and broker custom tests. Members trade their data for access.
why_now: Defense demand for proliferated LEO and a wave of well-funded satellite makers are stressing limited test capacity. Commercial-parts-first design is now standard.
revenue_model: $10-50k per year per member. 10-15% fee on brokered custom tests. Sponsored testing from chip vendors.
non_obvious_insight: In a commercial-parts space industry, test data is the scarce asset, not the parts. The group that pools it becomes the standards-setter.
first_30_days: Contact two beam facilities about block-time pricing. Pre-sell five founding memberships to satellite builders at $10k each. Publish a free first report on one popular microcontroller or memory part to establish credibility.

title: Half-Pro Remodeling: Homeowner Does the Easy 60%
one_liner: Fixed-price booking of only the licensed, permit-required slice of a project while homeowners or handymen do demo, prep and finish, with photo-verified handoffs.
customer: Budget-constrained homeowners with $3-15K bath, kitchen, water-heater, mini-split and electrical projects. Supply side: solo licensed plumbers and electricians who want prequalified, ready-to-work half-day jobs.
problem: Angi data shows 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects and 72% of postponers cite budget. The average project is $5,368. DIY-only fell from 50% to 39% while homeowner-plus-pro rose from 27% to 46%. Pros say they are too busy and skip small, messy, scope-uncertain jobs. Platforms sell whole jobs, so homeowners get no quotes.
solution: A catalog of standardized pro steps: rough-in for a vanity swap, shutoff valve and supply lines, gas line, water heater swap, ceiling-fan or lighting circuit, mini-split hookup, permit pull and inspection sign-off. Each comes with a homeowner checklist (nine prep steps, three photos) checked by a vision model, and a pro shows up for a fixed price to a job that is actually ready. Start only where owner-builder and licensing rules are clear.
why_now: Angi's 2026 backlog data. Credit cards rose to 30% of project payments. 62% now choose repair over replace. Contractors are capacity-constrained. Multimodal models can verify prep photos cheaply.
revenue_model: 15-20% take on the pro-step price ($300-1,500), plus materials affiliate margin from a local supply house. Pros pay nothing upfront.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of demand is not the project, it is the licensed hour. The blended-work data says homeowners do not want turnkey, they want to transfer risk only on the parts they legally or practically cannot do. Nobody sells the licensed two hours with a photo-checked handoff, and small pros love the productivity of arriving at a ready job.
first_30_days: One metro, four job types. Recruit 10 solo plumbers and electricians from local trade Facebook groups. Launch a landing page with local ads. Run 30 bookings by hand with a spreadsheet and Stripe.

title: Conversion X-Ray: Scan and Warrant Hidden Risks
one_liner: A 10-day scan of vacant office buildings (LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar, riser mapping) with an AI cost-risk budget, evolving into a cost-overrun warranty backed by the data.
customer: Buyers of distressed office evaluating conversion, their construction and mezzanine lenders, and later sureties and insurers.
problem: Conversions fail on unknowns: slab thickness and post-tension cables, asbestos and fireproofing, riser locations, window operability, structural transfers. Buyers price with averages and blow budgets by 20-40%, and lenders demand large contingencies or refuse.
solution: A rapid package for 40-300k sf buildings: handheld or drone LiDAR, GPR on slabs, facade thermal imaging, MEP riser mapping and sample testing. An AI cost-risk model outputs a per-unit cost distribution and a P80 budget in 10 days. As actual-versus-predicted data accumulates, offer a warranty or overrun cover.
why_now: $39B of office debt matures within 12 months and the buyer pool needs faster diligence. Handheld SLAM LiDAR and vision models are cheap, and public-land and affordable conversions require cost certainty.
revenue_model: $0.30-0.90 per sf for the scan, later warranty premiums of 1-2% of hard cost or lender-paid programs.
non_obvious_insight: Every conversion overrun is a data point that nobody collects. The first firm to log predicted-versus-actual cost across 50 conversions owns the only actuarial dataset in a market that insurers cannot yet price, so the scan is the loss leader for an insurance-like margin.
first_30_days: Buy a handheld LiDAR and rent a GPR unit. Scan three buildings at a discount for buyers in bid periods. Publish 'the top 10 hidden conversion killers' and sign two paid scans at about $15K each.
